items.stem: What does the processor do in the fetch–decode–execute cycle?
options: Fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it and carries it out
items.answer: Fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it and carries it out

items.stem: Distinguish between RAM and secondary storage.
items.answer: RAM is fast, volatile primary memory for data currently in use; secondary storage (SSD/HDD) is slower, non-volatile and keeps data permanently.
items.markingKey: RAM is fast, volatile primary memory for data currently in use; secondary storage (SSD/HDD) is slower, non-volatile and keeps data permanently. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "More RAM always makes a computer faster." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Extra RAM helps only if the computer is running out of memory; beyond that, speed depends on the CPU, storage and software.
items.markingKey: Extra RAM helps only if the computer is running out of memory; beyond that, speed depends on the CPU, storage and software. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the role of the CPU, RAM and secondary storage when a student opens and edits a video on a laptop, and evaluate which upgrade would most improve their experience.
items.answer: Storage holds the video and editor; loaded into RAM; CPU/GPU process edits; bottlenecks: RAM (swapping), storage speed (HDD vs SSD), GPU for rendering; justify an upgrade.

items.stem: Briefly explain why access to GPUs has become a source of power in digital society.
items.answer: Training advanced AI models requires vast numbers of GPUs; a few firms (e.g. Nvidia as supplier, large cloud companies as buyers) control access, and governments impose export controls (e.g. US restrictions on chips to China), so compute shapes economic and geopolitical power.

items.stem: A computer has 8 GB of RAM. The operating system uses 3 GB, and the user opens a word processor (2.5 GB), a photo editor (1.2 GB), a web browser with tabs (2.5 GB). Calculate the RAM still free, and state what happens if programs need more RAM than is available.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "proprietary software"?

A computer built into a larger device to perform a dedicated function, such as in a washing machine, car or pacemaker
Software owned by a company whose source code is kept secret and whose use is restricted by licence, such as Microsoft Windows or Adobe Photoshop
Gordon Moore's observation (1965, revised 1975) that the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years
items.answer: Software owned by a company whose source code is kept secret and whose use is restricted by licence, such as Microsoft Windows or Adobe Photoshop

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "secondary storage"?
options: Hardware that sends data into a computer, such as a keyboard, microphone, camera or sensor
Computing embedded everywhere in everyday objects and environments, rather than only in desktop computers
Hardware that presents processed data to the user, such as a screen, speaker or printer
Non-volatile storage such as SSDs and hard drives that keeps data when the power is off
items.answer: Non-volatile storage such as SSDs and hard drives that keeps data when the power is off
items.markingKey: D. "secondary storage" is non-volatile storage such as SSDs and hard drives that keeps data when the power is off.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Software whose source code is publicly available and can be studied, modified and shared under an open licence, such as Linux or Firefox"?
items.answer: open-source software
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of open-source software.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Gordon Moore's observation (1965, revised 1975) that the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years"?
items.answer: Moore's law
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of Moore's law.

items.stem: Briefly explain why solid-state drives (SSDs) have largely replaced hard disk drives in laptops.
items.answer: SSDs have no moving parts, so they are faster, more durable, quieter and use less power, which suits portable devices, even though they cost more per gigabyte.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: SSDs have no moving parts, so they are faster, more durable, quieter and use less power, which suits portable devices, even though they cost more per gigabyte. items.stem: Explain the difference between open-source software and proprietary software.
items.answer: Open-source software publishes its source code for anyone to study, modify and share (Linux, LibreOffice); proprietary software keeps code secret and restricts use through licences (Windows, Photoshop).
items.markingKey: Open-source software publishes its source code for anyone to study, modify and share (Linux, LibreOffice); proprietary software keeps code secret and restricts use through licences (Windows, Photoshop). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a mainframe era and a mobile era.
items.answer: In the mainframe era computing was centralised in large machines owned by organisations and used by specialists; in the mobile era computing is personal, portable and connected, used by billions of individuals.
items.markingKey: In the mainframe era computing was centralised in large machines owned by organisations and used by specialists; in the mobile era computing is personal, portable and connected, used by billions of individuals. items.stem: Explain the difference between RAM and secondary storage.
items.answer: RAM is fast, volatile primary memory for data currently in use; secondary storage (SSD/HDD) is slower, non-volatile and keeps data permanently.
items.markingKey: RAM is fast, volatile primary memory for data currently in use; secondary storage (SSD/HDD) is slower, non-volatile and keeps data permanently. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why proprietary software companies can exercise power over users.
items.answer: They control updates, file formats, pricing and which devices are supported, so users and organisations become dependent (lock-in) and must accept licence terms and data collection.

items.stem: The processor in a smartphone runs at 3.6 GHz and has 8 cores. Calculate the number of clock cycles per second for one core, and for all cores together.
items.answer: 3.6 × 10⁹ cycles per second per core; 2.88 × 10¹⁰ for all cores

items.stem: Briefly describe Munich's LiMux project and explain what it reveals about trade-offs between open-source and proprietary software.
items.answer: Munich moved thousands of city computers from Windows to Linux (LiMux) from 2004, but the city council voted in 2017 to return to Windows, citing compatibility problems. The switch saved licence costs and reduced lock-in, but compatibility and user resistance showed the strength of proprietary ecosystems.

items.stem: The Intel 8086 (1978) had about 29,000 transistors. Assuming Moore's law (transistor counts double every two years), estimate the number of transistors on a chip 30 years later.
items.answer: about 9.5 × 10⁸

items.stem: Using the global chip shortage (2020–2023) as an example, explain interdependence of hardware supply chains.
items.answer: Pandemic demand and supply disruptions caused shortages of semiconductors, forcing car makers to cut production. Many industries depend on a few chip manufacturers (e.g. TSMC in Taiwan), so disruption in one place affected economies worldwide.
items.markingKey: Context (Pandemic demand and supply disruptions caused shortages of semiconductors, forcing car makers to cut production.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Using Heartbleed (2014) as an example, explain the sustainability of open-source infrastructure.
items.answer: A bug in OpenSSL, open-source encryption software maintained by a handful of volunteers, exposed data on a large share of web servers. Critical infrastructure depended on under-funded volunteers, leading to the Core Infrastructure Initiative to fund key projects.

items.stem: The Intel Pentium (1993) had about 3,100,000 transistors. Assuming Moore's law (transistor counts double every two years), estimate the number of transistors on a chip 20 years later.
items.answer: about 3.17 × 10⁹

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"About 90% of the world's most advanced chips are made by one company on one island."
— Report on semiconductor supply chains, 2022 (referring to TSMC in Taiwan)

Explain one implication of the situation described in the source.
items.answer: Concentrated production creates vulnerability: a natural disaster, conflict or blockade affecting Taiwan could disrupt the global supply of advanced chips, so governments subsidise domestic production (e.g. US CHIPS Act 2022).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Governments should use only open-source software."
items.answer: Open source should be preferred where viable, but a pragmatic mix is often necessary; policies like "public money, public code" are a balanced approach.

items.stem: "Smartphones have been the most significant development in the history of computing." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Smartphones are arguably the most socially significant development so far because of their reach, though they built on earlier breakthroughs.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: brought computing and internet to billions, including in low-income countries; enabled new economies (apps, mobile money, gig work). items.stem: "The most important component of a computer for digital society is its processor." Discuss.
items.answer: Processors are crucial, but impacts depend on the whole system – storage, networks, interfaces and software.

items.stem: "Operating systems give technology companies more power than any app." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Control of the operating system is a particularly strong form of power because it sits beneath all apps, though it is increasingly challenged by regulators.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: control of app stores, defaults and permissions; iOS/Android duopoly on mobile. Arguments against: regulation (DMA) forces openness; apps with network effects (WhatsApp) also have huge power; web apps bypass OS stores.
